title: Search in Infinite Sorted Array
statement:
You have a sorted array `arr` of distinct integers whose length is **not known in advance**: think of it as infinite. Positions `0 .. n - 1` hold the given values in strictly increasing order, and every position `n` or beyond holds a value larger than any target (a sentinel `+∞`), so you can read any index safely but you do not know where the real data ends.

For each of `q` queries, find the index of the target value in `arr`, or report `-1` if it is not present.

The program receives the array in full so that it can be tested, but solve it as the interviewer intended: a linear scan, or a binary search with a hard-coded huge right end, is not acceptable. Locate a window `[lo, hi]` that must contain the target by **doubling** the right end (`1, 2, 4, 8, ...`) until `arr[hi]` is at least the target, then binary search inside that window. A single query must take `O(log p)` probes, where `p` is the position of the target (or of the first value not smaller than it).

**Follow-up:** the interviewer asked why the window should double rather than triple or grow by a constant, and to derive the complexity. Explain why doubling is a good balance between the number of expansion steps and the size of the final binary search, and show that the total cost is `O(log p)`.
inputFormat:
The first line contains `n`.
The second line contains `n` strictly increasing integers: `arr[0], ..., arr[n-1]`.
The third line contains `q`.
Each of the next `q` lines contains one integer: a target value.
outputFormat: Print `q` lines. Line `j` is the index of the `j`-th target in `arr`, or `-1` if it does not occur.

examples.explanation: 9 is at index 4, -5 at index 0 and 31 at index 7. The values 3 and 100 are not in the array.
The array holds just the value 7, at index 0.

hints: A plain binary search needs a right end. Instead of guessing a huge one, find it: start with hi = 1 and keep doubling it while arr[hi] is still smaller than the target.
Once arr[hi] is at least the target, the target (if present) lies in (hi / 2, hi]. Positions at or beyond n act as +infinity, so the loop always stops.
Binary search inside the last window. The doubling phase takes O(log p) steps and the window has size O(p), so the whole query is O(log p).
